tier_reason: The wiki Benchmarks tables compare z88dk builds against SDCC 4.6.0 #16608, HI-TECH C 3.09/7.80 and IAR 4.06A, and every row is backed by public code in support/benchmarks/<benchmark>/ (base source plus per-compiler subdirectories whose readme.txt gives the exact command lines, compiler versions and the z88dk-ticks invocation). The 'hardware' is a cycle-exact Z80 emulator, so the counts are deterministic per binary and fully reproducible.

corrections.claimed_speedup: From the wiki Benchmarks tables, Z80 cycles for SDCC 4.6.0 against z88dk's zsdcc 4.6.0 #16639 builds: n-Body 4,361,393,645 vs 2,243,368,504 for Z88DK/SDCC_CLASSIC (math48), 1.94x fewer (derived from page data), and vs 860,188,405 for Z88DK/SDCC_CLASSIC/MATH32, 5.07x (derived); the fastest z88dk n-Body row, Z88DK/SCCZ80_NEW/MATH32 at 807,783,742, is 5.40x (derived). Whetstone 1,850,296,726 vs 916,750,272 for Z88DK/SDCC_CLASSIC, 2.02x (derived), and vs 360,608,050 for Z88DK/SDCC/MATH32, 5.13x (derived). Fasta 414,019,207 vs 241,418,675 for Z88DK/SDCC_CLASSIC, 1.71x (derived). Pi without ldiv 7,218,092,827 vs 4,010,854,332 for Z88DK/SDCC_NEW, 1.80x (derived), and vs 1,696,878,309 for Z88DK/SCCZ80_NEW_FAST, 4.25x (derived). Dhrystone 2.1 274,542,684 vs 242,442,688 for Z88DK/SDCC_NEW, 1.13x (derived). Binary-Trees 193,466,493 vs 149,280,700 for Z88DK/SDCC_CLASSIC, 1.30x (derived). The Pi and Dhrystone comparison rows are the NEW library, not the classic library as the record said.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Baseline SDCC 4.6.0 #16608 (Linux), e.g. n-Body: 'sdcc -mz80 -DSTATIC -DTIMER --max-allocs-per-node200000 n-body.c' then makebin, timed with 'z88dk-ticks n-body.bin -start 0d7a -end 0dc0' (support/benchmarks/n-body/sdcc/readme.txt); Pi and Dhrystone use the same sdcc flags (Dhrystone adds -DNOSTRUCTASSIGN). z88dk classic zsdcc 4.6.0 #16639: 'zcc +test -vn -DSTATIC -DTIMER -D__Z88DK -compiler=sdcc -SO3 --max-allocs-per-node200000 n-body.c -o n-body.bin -lmath48 -m -lndos' (math32 rows use --math32); sccz80 classic math32: 'zcc +test -vn -DSTATIC -DTIMER -D__Z88DK -O2 n-body.c -o n-body.bin --math32 -m -lndos' (support/benchmarks/n-body/z88dk-classic/readme.txt). The __Z88DK define only enables intrinsic.h and printf/scanf options; it does not change the computation.
corrections.license: Clarified Artistic License (SPDX ClArtistic: FSF-libre and GPL-compatible but not OSI-approved per the SPDX license list), 'unless otherwise stated in the appropriate file'
corrections.caveats: The win is not uniform. With the NEW library Binary-Trees takes 6,570,984,020 cycles against 193,466,493 for plain SDCC (about 34x slower; the wiki blames the fast-realloc free-block search, issue #113), while the classic library is 1.30x faster. On Sieve the sccz80 builds (4.77M to 4.96M cycles) are slower than SDCC (4,218,689) and only Z88DK/SDCC_NEW (3,679,114) wins, by 1.15x and barely ahead of IAR (3,714,152); on Fannkuch HI-TECH C 7.80 is fastest and smallest (51,982,515 cycles, 868 bytes), sccz80 is slower than SDCC and SDCC_NEW wins by only 1.06x. The large n-Body, Whetstone, Fasta and Pi gains come mostly from z88dk's assembly-language float and 32-bit integer libraries replacing SDCC's C-implemented ones (the wiki says so), since zsdcc is z88dk's patched build of the same SDCC 4.6.0. Rows without a MATH32 label use pre-v2.5 genmath or math48 (48-bit) libraries and are not comparable to MATH32 rows; rows come from different dates (sccz80 NEW April 2021, sccz80 classic January 2022, zsdcc and SDCC August-September 2026). All results, including the HI-TECH C and IAR runs, were measured by the z88dk project itself. HI-TECH C 7.80 gives wrong Fasta output (DISQ). The baseline is a C compiler, not GNU as, NASM or MASM, and the z80asm assembler itself is not benchmarked, so the fit to assemblers-and-asm-tooling is weak. Clarified Artistic License is not OSI-approved and individual files may carry other licences.

notes: All quoted cycle counts match the wiki tables (raw wiki markdown read) and the per-compiler readme.txt RESULT blocks; only the library labels for the Pi and Dhrystone rows were wrong. Category fit is weak: this is a C toolchain-plus-library comparison, so the orchestrator may want a category override to a compilers category; usability moved to reference because ClArtistic is not OSI-approved (SPDX isOsiApproved false).

tier_reason: The PPoPP 2017 paper (sgemm.pdf in the repo, ACM ISBN 978-1-4503-4493-7) states on a Tesla K20m that the SGEMM reaches 3.1 Tflop/s (88%) against cuBLAS 7.0's 2.7 Tflop/s (76%) at 12288 x 12288, a 1.15x speedup, and that the convolution is 39%, 46% and 62% faster than cuDNN v4.0. It is peer-reviewed, but the repo holds only the .sass kernels, the assembler and the solver, with no timing harness or run scripts, so it is not A.

corrections.license: No repository-wide licence. KeplerAs/LICENSE is MIT (Copyright 2014 Scott Gray, 2015~2016 Xiuxia Zhang); the SGEMM .sass kernels carry 'Copyright 2015~2017 Xiuxia Zhang ... All rights reserved' lines (commit 'Added licence information', 2017-05-24), and one kernel file carries an Apache-2.0 header.
corrections.hardware: NVIDIA Tesla K20m (Kepler, 13 SMs); host CPU model not stated in the paper text read
corrections.caveats: This is a peer-reviewed PPoPP 2017 paper ('Understanding the GPU Microarchitecture to Achieve Bare-Metal Performance Tuning', originally 'Demystifying GPU Microarchitecture to Tune SGEMM'), but the repo has no benchmark harness, timing code or run scripts, and the convolution kernels behind the cuDNN claim are not in the repo at all (only KeplerAs, SGEMM and Solver directories). The paper says the 12x12 and 8x8 kernels beat cuBLAS 'in most cases' (8x8 is better at small sizes, the gain grows with matrix size), so 1.15x is the best large-matrix figure, not a uniform one. cuBLAS 7.0 and cuDNN 4.0 (2015-2016) and the Kepler-only ISA encoding are long obsolete. KeplerAs is a Perl assembler (Makefile.PL, lib/KeplerAs) derived from Scott Gray's MaxAs, which is listed separately in wave 13; the measured artifact is hand-written SASS against a vendor library, not an assembler-versus-assembler test. The kernels are 'All rights reserved' and only the assembler is MIT.

notes: Numbers verified in the repo's sgemm.pdf (pdftotext): 3.1 vs 2.7 Tflop/s, 88% vs 76%, 1.15x, and 39%/46%/62% over cuDNN v4.0. Not a duplicate of MaxAs (NervanaSystems/maxas): KeplerAs targets a different ISA (Kepler) using encodings from the authors' solver and has its own paper claim. Usability moved to mixed: MIT assembler, all-rights-reserved kernels.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. K2 is an ACM SIGCOMM 2021 paper (DOI 10.1145/3452296.3472929 in a search result), and its official artifact repo smartnic/sigcomm21_artifact restates the accepted paper's numbers against clang -O3 and ships reproduction scripts (4_reproduce_results: insn_count.sh, eq_chk.sh, the TRex run_mlffr_user.py flow). The paper PDF itself could not be opened (arXiv and par.nsf.gov are blocked), the clang version and CPU models are not stated on the pages opened, and the latency rerun needs reviewer-only CloudLab credentials, so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Artifact README (accepted-paper abstract, submission version): relative to clang -O3, 6-26% smaller code, 13-85 microseconds lower latency and -0.03 to 5% higher throughput (packets per second per core) on Cilium and Linux kernel programs. Camera-ready abstract (arXiv 2103.00022, search snippet only): 6-26% smaller code, 1.36%-55.03% lower average packet-processing latency and 0-4.75% higher throughput than the best clang-compiled program, on Cilium, Facebook and Linux kernel programs. The artifact's reference instruction-count table shows 6.25-16.67% fewer instructions than -O2/O3 on 11 benchmarks (e.g. xdp_devmap_xmit 36 to 30, sys_enter_open 24 to 20).
corrections.baseline: clang BPF output: -O3 per the abstract, and the best of the clang -O1/-O2/-O3 variants per benchmark in the throughput runs (the artifact example's best clang variant for xdp_map_access is O1); clang version not stated on the pages opened
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Baseline clang BPF builds at -O1/-O2/-O3 (version not stated on the pages opened). K2 is built from superopt with z3 at a pinned commit ('make main_ebpf.out'). Reproduction scripts are in smartnic/sigcomm21_artifact (4_reproduce_results/1_insn_count/insn_count.sh, 2_eq_chk_time/eq_chk.sh, and the TRex-based run_mlffr_user.py on CloudLab).
corrections.hardware: Submitted-paper Table 2 ran on CloudLab d6515 (AMD) machines; the artifact replication uses CloudLab xl170 (Intel) machines with a TRex traffic generator on a second node. CPU models are not named on the pages opened.
corrections.caveats: The paper PDF was not opened (arXiv, ar5iv, par.nsf.gov and k2.cs.rutgers.edu are unreachable here); the camera-ready numbers are from a search snippet, while the artifact README carries the submission-version abstract with different latency and throughput figures. Throughput gains are tiny (-0.03 to 5%, i.e. sometimes slightly slower), and the artifact says rerun numbers will not match Table 2 because it moved from AMD d6515 to Intel xl170 machines; the latency/throughput rerun requires CloudLab credentials and disk images given only to SIGCOMM reviewers. The search is stochastic, so outputs vary between runs, and optimisation takes minutes to over 20 minutes per program (e.g. sys_enter_open 1564 s); the paper says programs over about 200 instructions cannot be optimised quickly. Not every K2 variant passes the kernel verifier (e.g. 4 of 5 for xdp2, xdp_router_ipv4 and xdp_redirect). The superopt README is install-only ('Todo: add more instructions soon'). The baseline is clang BPF output, not GNU as, NASM or MASM, so the fit to assemblers-and-asm-tooling is weak.

notes: The record's numbers match the camera-ready abstract (snippet only); the artifact README gives the submission-version figures (13-85 us lower latency, -0.03 to 5% throughput), and both are now in claimed_speedup. MIT licence (Srinivas Narayana, 2019), 30 stars and last commit 2021-09-16 (abandoned) are confirmed. A paper-access retier could check Table 2's clang version and CPU model, which might reach A, since the artifact code is public.
